messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 36

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Karim's Vigil

Karim was thirty-eight when his younger brother Samir was hit by a delivery truck outside their family's grocery store in Dearborn. The impact happened in an instant—Samir stepping into the street, the sound Karim could never quite describe, the way his brother's body moved in a way bodies should not move. By the time Karim reached him, Samir's left leg was bent at an angle that made Karim's mind refuse to process what he was seeing. The blood pooled on the asphalt, and there was a smell—not quite copper, not quite anything Karim had encountered in his fourteen years as a paramedic. It was the smell of exposure, of something interior made suddenly exterior. He had worked the code himself, his hands performing the motions while his mind fractured into two parts: the paramedic who knew the protocols, and the brother who was losing Samir.

Samir survived, but barely. He spent six weeks in the hospital, and those weeks became the architecture of Karim's new life. He visited every shift he could, and the hospital smell—that particular blend of bleach and something medicinal that Karim had never noticed before—began to live in his nostrils. It followed him home. It was in his clothes, in his hair, in the fabric of his car. Two years later, he still caught it sometimes when he walked past a pharmacy, and his chest would tighten as if the truck were coming again.

Work became impossible and indispensable at once. Karim would volunteer for extra shifts, telling his wife Leila that the overtime was for Samir's ongoing physical therapy bills, though the medical debt had long since been managed. The truth was that sitting at home meant thinking, and thinking meant the memory would arrive whole and complete—not just the visual of Samir's leg, but the smell, the particular quality of the sunlight that afternoon, the sound of someone screaming, though he could not now remember if that someone was himself. When the memory came, it came with a terror so immediate and so total that Karim's body would respond as though the truck were hitting Samir again in that very moment. His hands would shake. His breath would come in short bursts. He would have to leave the room, leave the house sometimes, just to escape the sensation that he was standing on that street again.

The work itself had become different. A month ago, Karim responded to a call for a construction accident—a man with a visible laceration on his forearm, nothing severe by any measure. The moment Karim saw the wound, something in his vision narrowed. He could not look at it directly. He found himself assigning the bandaging to his junior partner, something he had never done in fourteen years. His partner had noticed. So had his supervisor. There had been conversations about "fitness for duty," words that made Karim feel as though he were failing at the one thing he had always been competent at.

At home, Leila had learned not to touch him without warning. Two months ago, she had placed her hand on his shoulder while he sat at the kitchen table, and he had flinched so violently that he knocked over his coffee. The shame of that moment—of his wife having to apologize for touching him—had lodged somewhere in his chest. He had come to believe that something fundamental in him had broken that day on the street, that he was no longer the man Leila had married, no longer someone she could rely on. He would sit in the living room and choose his seat based on what he could see, where his back was protected, which exit was closest. He was aware of how this looked, how paranoid it seemed, and yet he could not stop doing it.

He could not remember the exact moment the truck hit—there was a gap there, a blank space his mind refused to fill. But he remembered everything else with a clarity that felt like torture. He had tried, for months, to suppress the thoughts, to push them away through sheer force of will, but they would return unbidden, complete and overwhelming. Last week, his supervisor had suggested he take medical leave. Karim had finally agreed. He was sitting in his living room, in his chosen safe seat, when he called to make an appointment with a therapist. What he wanted most was to stop being afraid. What he feared most was that the person he had been before that day was simply gone.
